title: Letter III

teacherSummary.text: A brief letter: Walton reports that he is safe and well advanced on his voyage. He is full of confidence and determination despite floating ice.

vocabulary.definition: Having no beaten path or way
vocabulary.context: Thus far I have gone, tracing a secure way over the pathless seas: the very stars themselves being witnesses and testimonies of my triumph.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “pathless”: path (Greek pathos, "feeling, suffering") + -less (Old English -leas, "without"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The act of one who traces
vocabulary.context: Thus far I have gone, tracing a secure way over the pathless seas: the very stars themselves being witnesses and testimonies of my triumph.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “tracing”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I am, however, in good spirits: my men are bold, and apparently firm of purpose; nor do the floating sheets of ice that continually pass us, indicating the dangers of the region towards which we are advancing, appear to dismay them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “indicate”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Being in the direction of home
vocabulary.context: This letter will reach England by a merchantman now on its homeward voyage from Archangel; more fortunate than I, who may not see my native land, perhaps, for many years.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “homeward”: ard (Latin ardere, "to burn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Falling or striking upon, as a ray of light upon a reflecting surface
vocabulary.context: No incidents have hitherto befallen us that would make a figure in a letter.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “incident”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: One or two stiff gales, and the springing of a leak, are accidents which experienced navigators scarcely remember to record; and I shall be well content if nothing worse happen to us during our voyage.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “accident”: ac- (Latin ad, "to") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Subject in will or act to authority
vocabulary.context: Why not still proceed over the untamed yet obedient element?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “obedient”: ob- (Latin ob, "against, toward") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Buoyed upon or in a fluid
vocabulary.context: I am, however, in good spirits: my men are bold, and apparently firm of purpose; nor do the floating sheets of ice that continually pass us, indicating the dangers of the region towards which we are advancing, appear to dismay them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “floating”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Sagacious in adapting means to ends
vocabulary.context: I will be cool, persevering, and prudent.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “prudent”: -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I am, however, in good spirits: my men are bold, and apparently firm of purpose; nor do the floating sheets of ice that continually pass us, indicating the dangers of the region towards which we are advancing, appear to dismay them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “advance”: ad- (Latin ad, "to, toward"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Short letters between long ones create pacing and suspense, a technique common in epistolary fiction.

significance: Walton's optimism makes the coming crisis feel more dramatic and ironic.
discussionQuestions: Why might Shelley include such a short, cheerful letter here?
Where does tone / mood appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the sublime power of nature?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Letter III,” how does Shelley show confidence before danger? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the tone / mood you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Letter III develops the idea of confidence before danger. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of tone / mood and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses tone / mood in Letter III to complicate the reader's understanding of confidence before danger. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Letter III within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of confidence before danger responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Letter III as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of confidence before danger. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood
annotationFocus.lookFor: word choices that reveal the narrator's attitude or the scene's feeling
annotationFocus.passage: No incidents have hitherto befallen us that would make a figure in a letter. One or two stiff gales, and the springing of a leak, are accidents which experienced navigators scarcely remember to record; and I shall be well content if nothing worse happen to us during our voyage.

annotationFocus.label: Foreshadowing
annotationFocus.lookFor: hints, warnings or images that point to later events

annotationFocus.label: Setting
annotationFocus.lookFor: where and when events happen and how place shapes action or feeling

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why might Shelley include such a short, cheerful letter here? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are pathless, tracing, indicating, homeward, incidents. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Thus far I have gone, tracing a secure way over the pathless seas: the very stars themselves being witnesses and testimonies of my triumph.” Webster's says: Having no beaten path or way. Now the word history: “pathless”: path (Greek pathos, "feeling, suffering") + -less (Old English -leas, "without"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “tracing”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it. “indicate”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Short letters between long ones create pacing and suspense, a technique common in epistolary fiction. Why does this chapter matter? Walton's optimism makes the coming crisis feel more dramatic and ironic. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for tone / mood.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see tone / mood, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to confidence before danger.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Tone / mood, Foreshadowing, Setting.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of tone / mood. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: No incidents have hitherto befallen us that would make a figure in a letter. One or two stiff gales, and the springing of a leak, are accidents which experienced navigators scarcely remember to record; and I shall be well content if nothing worse happen to us during our voyage.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Tone / mood, Foreshadowing, Setting: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Letter III,” how does Shelley show confidence before danger? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the tone / mood you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about confidence before danger, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how tone / mood shapes confidence before danger. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
